Alright, the recent series of actions have gotten me to a point where the subagent delegation logic in `src/core/agent.ts` has been patched and rebuilt successfully. The subagent now tracks executed tool calls to avoid infinite loops, and the latest build of the CLI (`glint`) has been installed to `~/.local/bin/glint`. I also verified that the subagent can correctly enumerate the tool names from `src/core/tools.ts`, confirming that the tool registration and subagent invocation mechanisms are working as intended.

The next feature I want to test is the ability to take screenshots of web pages using the Playwright integration that the CLI provides. The `screenshot` tool (or a similar tool) ultimately relies on an underlying browser executable (Chromium, Chrome, Firefox, etc.) that Playwright can launch. If no suitable browser is installed, any attempt to run the screenshot command will fail with an obscure error about missing browsers, which would be a dead end and waste time debugging later.

Before I go ahead and craft a prompt that asks the subagent (or the CLI directly) to screenshot a site, I should first verify the environment: 
1. Which browser binaries are actually present on this system (`chromium`, `chromium-browser`, `google-chrome`, `firefox`)? 
2. Whether Playwright has already downloaded any browser binaries into its cache directory (`~/.cache/ms-playwright`). If the cache exists, I can get a quick sense of which browsers Playwright thinks are available.

A simple way to do this is to run a Bash command that checks the `which` locations for the common browser executables, suppressing errors, and then lists the first few entries in the Playwright cache directory (if it exists). This will give me a concise snapshot of the environment without pulling in unnecessary output.

Given the tooling available, the appropriate approach is a `Bash` tool call with the command:
```
which chromium chromium-browser google-chrome firefox 2>/dev/null; ls ~/.cache/ms-playwright 2>/dev/null | head -3
```
The `2>/dev/null` part silences any “not found” messages from `which`, and the `ls | head -3` limits the output to the first three entries, which is enough to confirm the presence of any downloaded browsers.

I’ll label the description accordingly so it’s clear why I’m running this: “Check for browsers to screenshot website”. This will set the stage for the next step, where I can safely invoke the screenshot tool knowing the necessary browser binaries are in place.

Thus, the next action is to issue this Bash command via the tool.

arguments.command: which chromium chromium-browser google-chrome firefox 2>/dev/null; ls ~/.cache/ms-playwright 2>/dev/null | head -3
arguments.description: Check for browsers to screenshot website
